summary: Describes how an EPP session is mapped onto a single TCP connection. It requires Transport Layer Security to protect the information exchanged between EPP client and server. It obsoletes an earlier version and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5734 explains how an EPP conversation runs over a single TCP connection. Each message carries its own length, and TLS protects the connection and checks the identities of both machines.

questions: how does epp run over tcp
how are epp messages framed over tcp
subtitle: How an EPP session uses one TCP connection, length-prefixed messages and TLS protection.

tldr.problem: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) needs a transport mapping that preserves its client-server sessions and delimits messages on a TCP connection. EPP credentials also need protection while in transit.
tldr.mechanism: Each EPP session uses one TCP connection. Each data unit starts with a 32-bit total length, and the connection must use TLS with mutual certificate authentication.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5734 defines the EPP TCP transport and requires TLS protection. It obsoletes RFC 4934 and is updated by RFC 8996.

facts.label: TLS authentication
facts.value: Mutual client and server authentication is required

today: RFC 5734 is Internet Standard STD 69, published in August 2009. It obsoletes RFC 4934 and has been updated by RFC 8996.

sections.title: One Connection per EPP Session
sections.content:
An EPP session maps to one TCP connection between a client and a server. The client opens the connection to the standard TCP port assigned by IANA. Once connected, the server must send an EPP <greeting>.

A session normally ends when the client sends <logout>. The server must end the session and close the TCP connection. A client may close the connection to end the session. A server may also close connections after a server-defined idle period or maximum lifetime.

A client may open multiple connections for multiple EPP sessions, but commands from one session must not be split across connections.
sections.plainLanguage: Each EPP session stays on its own TCP connection. The server greets the client after connection, and logout normally ends the session and closes that connection.

sections.title: Commands and Responses
sections.content:
Except for the server greeting, the client starts EPP messages with commands. The server must return each response on the same TCP connection. Commands are processed independently and in the order the client sent them.

A client may pipeline commands by sending a later command before receiving the earlier response. Pipelining does not change EPP's basic command-response operation. Each data unit must contain exactly one EPP message, so a client cannot combine several commands in one data unit.

If the connection closes after a command has been processed but before its response reaches the client, the server may try to undo the command's effects. EPP commands are idempotent: processing one more than once has the same net effect as processing it once.
sections.plainLanguage: A client sends commands, and the server replies on the same connection. Commands may be sent ahead of their replies, but each message stays separate and the server processes them in order.

sections.title: The EPP Data Unit
sections.content:
Every EPP data unit has a 32-bit Total Length field followed by one EPP XML instance. The length is measured in octets, uses network (big-endian) byte order, and includes the four octets of the length field itself.

The receiver subtracts four octets from the total to determine the XML instance length. It must read that many octets before processing the EPP message. This length prefix marks the boundary of each message in the TCP data stream.
sections.plainLanguage: A message begins with a number that gives its full size, including the number itself. The receiver reads that many bytes to find the end of the XML message.

sections.title: TLS Handshake and Certificate Checks
sections.content:
The client connects and starts a TLS handshake before sending EPP data. Both sides must authenticate each other with certificates, validate the certification paths and certificate details, and complete the handshake before EPP service is granted. The parties must agree out of band on acceptable certificate identities.

The client must compare the server's certificate identity with its expected server name or address before sending login credentials. For a server name, the profile uses a dNSName subjectAltName when present; a wildcard may appear only as the left-most DNS label. The Common Name may be used as a fallback, although the RFC describes it as deprecated. For an IP address, the client compares the address with an iPAddress subjectAltName.

All EPP messages must be sent as TLS application data. A message may span TLS records, and a TLS record may contain multiple EPP messages. When closing an idle connection, the server must try to exchange TLS close_notify alerts first.
sections.plainLanguage: Before login, the client checks the server's certificate and both machines authenticate through TLS. EPP messages then travel inside the protected TLS connection.

sections.title: Why the Connection Must Be Protected
sections.content:
EPP by itself uses client identifiers and plain-text passwords. A passive observer could recover them and use them to forge commands. The TCP mapping therefore requires TLS to provide integrity, confidentiality and mutual strong client-server authentication.

The TLS certificate authenticates the client and server machines. The EPP identifier and password authenticate the client's user identity, which may differ from the identity in the client certificate. Before sending credentials, the client must check the server certificate and confirm that its identity information agrees with the EPP greeting.

The RFC also notes that EPP TCP servers can face TCP denial-of-service attacks such as SYN flooding. It recommends steps such as firewalls and border-router filters to restrict inbound access to trusted clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Without TLS, someone listening could capture EPP passwords and forge commands. TLS protects the messages and lets each machine check the identity of the other.
